note: The #open_claims temp table becomes a DataFrame.
snippet:
SELECT c.claim_id,
               c.claim_number,
               UPPER(RTRIM(c.lob_code)) AS lob_code,
               c.reported_date
        INTO   #open_claims
        FROM   stg.claims AS c WITH (NOLOCK)
        WHERE  c.status IN ('OPEN', 'REOPENED')
          AND  c.reported_date <= @AsOfDate;

note: status is VARCHAR(12). Under the CI collation, IN ('OPEN','REOPENED') also matches 'Open' and 'reopened'. Spark's isin is case-sensitive and would drop those claims.
status is VARCHAR. Values stored with trailing spaces, such as 'OPEN ', still match in SQL Server but not with an exact match in Spark.

note: The claim_cur cursor loop handles one claim at a time and inserts into #aging. It becomes a set-based left join and aggregation per claim.

The nested pay_cur loop carries n_pay, total and last_pay from row to row in payment_date, payment_id order. It becomes count, sum and max per claim. Claims with no payments must get n_payments=0, total_paid=0 (not NULL) and last_payment_date NULL.

note: Latent: amount is nullable. One NULL amount makes @total NULL for the rest of that claim's loop and in the output, while Spark's sum skips NULLs. n_pay still counts that row. last_pay is the date of the last payment in order, which equals the max payment_date.
DATEDIFF(DAY) on DATE values is the plain day difference, so the value is safe. But Spark's datediff(end, start) takes its arguments in reverse order.
DATEDIFF(WEEK) counts the Sundays crossed between reported_date and @AsOfDate, not elapsed weeks. floor(datediff/7) would be wrong.
